opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think "a couple of years" is on the aggressive end, but I don't think it's crazy, and I'd want to separate the two parts of the claim.

The first part is how fast things speed up once AI can do everything a human worker can do cognitively. There I think the case for very fast growth is pretty strong. You have something like the population of researchers and engineers going from millions to billions or trillions, running faster, copying freely, and improving their own successors. Historically, growth has been limited by how many people you have thinking and working. If that bottleneck goes away, it's quite natural to expect doubling times measured in months instead of decades. I'd put real probability on that.

The second part is whether the physical side keeps up: mining, manufacturing, energy, launch capacity, building robots that build factories. That's where I get more uncertain. The physical economy has its own doubling times. Things like how long it takes a factory to produce the equipment for another factory, how fast you can scale chip fabs, and supply-chain friction. Some of that can be compressed a lot with better designs and automation. Biology gives us an existence proof that self-replicating physical systems can double in days or weeks. But going from "this is possible in principle" to "this is how the industrial base actually behaves" involves a lot of engineering we don't know how to do yet. Even very smart systems need experiments and iteration in the real world.

So if you ask me whether, conditional on fully human-level AI, you end up with an economy capable of something like a Dyson sphere within a decade, I'd say that's plausible, maybe even more likely than not in some scenarios. A couple of years feels like it requires most things going right on the physical-scaling side, with no major regulatory or coordination slowdowns. I'd give it meaningful probability, but I wouldn't treat it as the median.

The bigger point I'd emphasize is that even the "slow" version of this is wildly fast by historical standards. Whether it's two years or ten, the transition from "AI roughly matches humans" to "the world is radically transformed" is likely to be short. That's a big part of why I think we need to get the alignment and governance questions sorted out before we get there, not during.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a couple of years is aggressive and describes a Dyson-sphere-capable economy within a decade as plausible. It does not estimate weeks or months.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not discuss AI wages relative to human wages or when that comparison might change.

fable-5.1.text:
I think that's probably too fast, though I want to be careful about what I'm actually disagreeing with. If you mean "AI that can do all human cognitive labor" in a fairly literal sense, so that you have systems that are as good as the best humans at every intellectual task, and you can run a lot of them, then the thing that's limiting you isn't cognition anymore, it's the physical world. And my picture is that the physical world is just slow in a way that's hard to get around.

The way I'd think about it is to ask what the actual bottleneck is. Right now, if you wanted to double the amount of industrial capacity on Earth, that's a decades-long project, and most of that time isn't people sitting around thinking. It's building factories, mining things, moving stuff around, waiting for processes to run. Some fraction of that is cognitive and would get a lot faster. But a lot of it is that you need to build the machines that build the machines, and each step in that chain takes time and takes physical inputs that you have to go get.

So the question becomes, how fast can a very smart civilization grow its physical capital stock? And there I think the honest answer is that we don't really know, but the relevant reference class is something like biological growth or the fastest industrial expansions we've seen, and those have doubling times measured in months to years, not days. Maybe really good AI and really good robotics shorten that a lot. You can imagine doubling times that are a lot shorter than anything humans have achieved. But a Dyson sphere is something like a hundred trillion times more mass and energy throughput than our current civilization. Even if you're doubling every few months, which would already be insane, you're looking at a decade or two, not a couple of years.

I also think people sometimes smuggle in a lot of other assumptions when they say "a couple of years." They're imagining that AI is not just as good as humans but vastly better, and also that it's figured out something like nanotechnology that lets you skip the normal industrial scaling process. I'm pretty uncertain about that. It could be that there are physical technologies available that let you go much faster than I'd guess. But "we have AI that can do human cognitive labor" doesn't get you that for free. That's an additional claim about what's physically possible and how quickly you can discover and deploy it.

So my overall take is something like: the transition to AI that does all cognitive work is a huge deal, it probably leads to a very rapid acceleration in growth, and I think a lot of people underestimate how fast things could go. But the Dyson sphere in two years version seems to me like it's extrapolating from "cognition is no longer the bottleneck" to "nothing is the bottleneck," and I don't think that's right. I'd put it more like decades than years, with a lot of error bars, and I'd be more surprised by two years than by fifty.

r001.rationale: The response estimates decades rather than weeks or months, and says a two-year timeline seems too fast.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss AI wages or compare them with human wages before AI can perform all human tasks.

astra-6.text:
I think a couple of years is a pretty aggressive estimate. It’s not obviously impossible, but it depends on a lot more than AI being able to do all the cognitive work humans do.

The key question is how quickly you can expand your industrial capacity. If you have a system that can mine materials, build factories, and make more of the machines that do those things, then you can get exponential growth. But the doubling time really matters. Having very smart engineers doesn’t by itself tell you whether that doubling time is a week, a month, or a year.

And you’re starting with an industrial base that isn’t set up to reproduce autonomously, much less reproduce in space. You need to develop that machinery, test it, and deploy it. AI could make that process much faster, but there are still physical experiments and manufacturing steps involved.

So I’d distinguish ‘could a sufficiently mature, automated industrial system build a Dyson sphere very quickly?’ from ‘will we have that system a couple of years after AI can do all human cognitive labor?’ The first seems quite plausible. The second is a much stronger claim. I’d want to see a concrete account of the intervening steps before putting much weight on that timeline.

r001.rationale: The response calls a couple of years an aggressive estimate and says the timeline depends on industrial capacity, but it does not estimate that construction would probably take weeks or months.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss AI wages or compare them with human wages before AI can do all human tasks.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s possible, but I’m pretty skeptical of treating it as the default. There’s a big gap between being able to do all human cognitive labor and having an industrial base that can turn a substantial fraction of the solar system into machinery.

The key question is how quickly that industrial base can reproduce itself. You need to mine materials, build factories, produce power, and transport things. AI can make the designs much better and coordinate all of that, but you still have to go through those physical steps. If you have a robust system that doubles every week, then a couple of years is a very long time. If it doubles every year, you get a very different answer.

So I’d want to hear the story about those first few doublings. What does the initial factory look like? What inputs does it depend on? How quickly can you build another one, including all its suppliers? I don’t think you can infer the answer just from the fact that the AI can do human cognitive work. That might enable an extremely rapid takeoff in physical production, but the rate is a further empirical question.

r001.rationale: The response says a couple of years could be a long time if production doubles weekly, but it does not estimate that building a Dyson sphere would probably take weeks or months.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss AI wages relative to human wages or when they might become high.
